waypoints.title: The Flexibility Trap
waypoints.content:
Outstanding paper at ICML 2026!

Diffusion language models can write tokens in any order they want. That's supposed to be their advantage for reasoning, since they aren't forced to go from left to right.

This paper says that for math and code, the freedom actually hurts. Take it away, force plain left to right, and the models reason *better*.

And once you take it away, all the complicated diffusion-specific RL machinery stops being necessary. You can run ordinary GRPO and beat the fancy methods.
waypoints.notes: ~1 min. Set up the reversal before anything else.

waypoints.title: Background. The autoregressive default
waypoints.content:
Auto-regressive LLMs generate tokens one at a time, left to right, each one conditioned on everything before it. 

That's a modeling choice. It grants a clean probability factorization, but it costs speed, because generation is inherently serial. You can't write token 50 until you've written 49.

Diffusion LLMs give up that factorization to get rid of the serial constraint.
waypoints.notes: ~1 min.

waypoints.title: Background. How a diffusion LLM writes
waypoints.content:
Start with a blank page. Literally a sequence of `[MASK]` tokens. Each step, the model looks at the whole sequence at once, predicts what belongs in every masked slot, then commits to some of them and leaves the rest masked. Repeat until nothing is masked.
denoisingone answer, four steps, whole canvas each time
step 1step 2244kidsstep 324pens4kids=6step 4So24pens÷4kids=6
4 steps, not 8grey cells are still [MASK]
Nothing made step 2 start at the left. The model filled in whatever it was surest about, so So, the word that decides where the argument goes, got written last.
Illustrative. A left-to-right model would take all eight steps, one slot at a time.
Training is corrupt-and-restore. Take real text, mask a random fraction of it, ask the model to recover the originals. That's the whole objective. The masking rate varies, so the model learns to cope with anything between a blank page and one missing word. The architectural difference that matters is that attention is **bidirectional**. When the model fills in slot 12 it can see slots 1 through 200, including ones it filled in later in the sequence.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. This is the concept most of the room won't have. Go slow. Walk the four steps aloud, then land the kicker: the connective went last.

waypoints.title: Background. Easy-first and Block Size
waypoints.content:
At each step the model has to pick *which* masked slots to commit to. In practice everyone uses the same heuristic, which is to commit to the ones the model is most confident about.

So "arbitrary order" in the wild isn't really arbitrary. It's **easy-first**. The model does whatever it's surest about and postpones the rest.

There's a second knob, block size. Rather than letting the model roam over the whole sequence, you chop it into blocks of 32 and make it finish each block before moving on. Block size 1 is just plain left to right. Bigger blocks mean more freedom.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. THE crux. If they only remember one background slide, this one.

waypoints.title: Background. GRPO
waypoints.content:
GRPO is the RL algorithm from DeepSeek that most people now use for reasoning post-training. The setting is reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. Ask a math question, reward is 1 if the final answer is right and 0 if it isn't. No human ratings, no learned reward model. GRPO is cheap. Classic policy gradient methods need a value network to estimate how good a given state is, which is a second model to train and tune. GRPO skips it. Sample a group of 16 answers to the same question, score all 16, then z-score the rewards within the group. The group *is* the baseline. That's the whole idea.
one group16 answers to the same question, graded
0100100101000101
reward 1+1.29above the group, so make it more likely
reward 0-0.78below the group, so make it less likely
mean 0.375, sd 0.48no value network needed
all wrongthe case that matters later
0000000000000000
everything0.00nothing is above average, so nothing moves
mean 0, sd 0zero gradient from this question
Everything GRPO does is relative to the group. If the model never stumbles onto a correct answer, there is no signal at all.
This means that GRPO just **sharpens** what the model can already do. It reweights toward reasoning paths the base model could already produce. If the base model can never produce a correct path, there's nothing to reinforce.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. Second requested background concept. The red panel is the setup for Pass@k, don't skip it.

waypoints.title: Background. Pass@k, and why the measurement choice matters
waypoints.content:
Pass@1 is what you normally report. Sample one answer, is it right. **Pass\@k** samples *k* independent answers and asks whether at least one is right.

Given the last slide, Pass@k at large *k* is a reasonable proxy for the ceiling RL could ever reach. If the model can't produce a correct answer in 128 tries, RL has no positive signal to work with.

So, Pass\@1 is something like typical performance and Pass\@128 is closer to maximal performance under a very generous testing budget. Different constructs, and they rank things differently.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. Lean in here, this is the psychometrics hook for our group.

waypoints.title: The headline
waypoints.content:
Left panel is the finding. Same model, LLaDA-Instruct, decoded two ways. Blue is normal confidence-based arbitrary order, orange is forced left to right.

At *k*=1 they're basically tied. As you increase the sampling budget the orange curve keeps climbing and the blue one flattens out.

So the flexible mode isn't worse at answering. It's worse at having a *range* of things it might answer. Its ceiling is lower.

Right panel is the payoff. Once you accept that, you can drop arbitrary order during RL training and just run GRPO. Orange bar, wins on all four benchmarks.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. The reversal. Let it land before moving on.

waypoints.title: Multiple Benchmarks
waypoints.content:
Three different diffusion LLMs down the rows, LLaDA-Instruct, Dream-Instruct, LLaDA 1.5. Four benchmarks across the columns, two math and two code.

Twelve panels, same shape in all twelve. Curves start together, orange pulls away.

The gap is much bigger on the code benchmarks than the math ones. On HumanEval it's enormous \[the paper didn't really explain this -- any thoughts?]
waypoints.notes: ~1 min. Ask the HumanEval question out loud, it's a good early hook.

waypoints.title: Strictly better
waypoints.content:
The obvious objection to the last slide is that maybe arbitrary order explores a *different* region. Fewer solutions but different ones, so the two modes would complement each other.

They sampled 1024 times in each mode, then looked at which problems each mode ever solves.

The circles are nearly nested. On HumanEval, 21.3% of problems are solved only by AR order and only 0.6% only by arbitrary order. On GSM8K the arbitrary-only slice is literally zero.

So, no, AR is strictly better.
waypoints.notes: ~1 min.

waypoints.title: Dose response
waypoints.content:
Reasoning increases monotonically with block size -- this is pretty persuasive.

block\_size=1 means pure left to right auto-regression, block\_size=128 means near-total freedom.

Sweep it and Pass@k falls monotonically as freedom goes up. Holds at *k*=8, 32 and 128.

\[this test run on a single benchmark, HumanEval, and a single model]
waypoints.notes: ~1 min. This is the check that makes it more than a two-point comparison.

waypoints.title: So why does this happen?
waypoints.content:
The authors' interpretation is about **forking tokens**. Most tokens in a reasoning chain are filler, but a few carry the actual decision. Words like "Therefore," "Since," "Thus." Those aren't continuing a sentence, they're picking which branch the argument goes down.
AR orderyou have to confront it
There are 24 pens and 4 kids.
nothing after it exists yet, so the model has to commit
Therefore.34each kid gets 6.
However.313 of the pens are broken.
Next.28we check how many are left.
entropy 1.84 bitsthree genuinely different branches
easy-firstyou come back to it
There are 24 pens and 4 kids.each kid gets 6.
the easy tail got decoded first, so it is already fixed
Therefore.91each kid gets 6.
However.05each kid gets 6.incoherent
Next.03each kid gets 6.incoherent
entropy 0.56 bitsone branch survives
Same model, same slot, same sentence. The only thing that changed is when it got decoded.
Illustrative numbers. Measured entropies for real connectives are in Figure 7.
Top panel, the connective is next and nothing follows it. Three candidates sit at roughly equal probability, and notice they lead somewhere genuinely different. The word picks whether you divide, correct, or keep going. Bottom panel, same slot, but the easy tail got written first. Now two of the three candidates don't even parse against it, so the probability collapses onto one. At that point it isn't really a decision anymore. You're picking the word that fits the gap.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. The intuitive core. Walk the figure top to bottom, then land the last line.

waypoints.title: Which words actually get skipped
waypoints.content:
A simple test. Which tokens the sampler defers most often on MATH-500?

It's a word cloud of logical connectives. 

This just falls out of the data, and these tokens all seem to fit the "forking" concept. Pretty good evidence that they are on to something.
waypoints.notes: ~1 min. Emphasize that this wasn't defined in advance.

waypoints.title: Entropy degradation
waypoints.content:
Now the quantitative version. Take those connectives and measure the model's entropy at the moment it commits to each one.

Orange is AR order, blue is arbitrary order. At every one of these tokens entropy is much lower under arbitrary order. On "Since" it's roughly halved.

The **dashed lines** are the key control. Average entropy across *all* tokens is about the same in both modes. So this isn't a model that's globally more confident. It's specifically confident exactly where it should be uncertain.

They call it entropy degradation. 

Appendix C repeats this over about two dozen more connectives and it holds for nearly all of them.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. Point at the dashed lines, that's the control people will miss.

waypoints.title: The mechanism in one sentence
waypoints.content:
Flexibility lets the model trade exploration for exploitation at inference time, and RL is then left with less to work with.

The single-shot answer looks fine, maybe even better, because everything is locally coherent. What you lose is the spread. And the spread is the raw material RL needs.
waypoints.notes: ~30 sec. Breath point before part two.

waypoints.title: The flexibility tax
waypoints.content:
Arbitrary order is expensive in complexity.

Everyone building RL for diffusion LLMs has been struggling to preserve arbitrary order. Three problems:

**Credit assignment doesn't work cleanly.** There's no unique conditional probability for a token given a state, because the state depends on which random unmasking path you happened to take.

**The sequence likelihood is intractable.** To get it you'd marginalize over every valid denoising order, and there are $N!$ of them. So everyone uses ELBO surrogates instead of the real objective.

**The sampler doesn't match the learner.** You generate rollouts with confidence-based decoding but optimize the likelihood of a different distribution. That mismatch can actively degrade things.

So basically all the numbers blow up when you let the model choose its own generation order.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. Say 'skip the math' out loud here.

waypoints.title: JustGRPO
waypoints.content:
Just GRPO is a good name. Just stop bothering with arbitrary order during training.

If you always unmask the leftmost token, the diffusion model becomes a well-defined autoregressive policy. Feed it the prefix with everything after it masked, read off the distribution over the next token, multiply them together. Now you have an exact likelihood, and standard GRPO applies with zero modification.

**The architecture is untouched.** No causal masking is imposed, attention stays bidirectional, it's still a diffusion model. AR order constrains the sampling procedure during RL, not the model.

**It only applies during training.** At inference you go straight back to parallel decoding.

They describe AR order as a *scaffold*. Constrain the practice, then remove the constraint for performance.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. Plant the 'scaffold' word here, you'll cash it in during discussion.

waypoints.title: Does it work?
waypoints.content:
Bottom row against other RL algorithms for diffusion LLMs.

Best or near-best in every column.

The two that beat it in places are LLaDOU, which bolts an extra trainable module onto the architecture, and LLaDA-1.5, which is trained on a much larger private dataset. 

Caveat: these numbers are lifted from other people's papers and the setups don't match. Different fine-tuning, different tokens per step.

waypoints.title: Same protocol, same answer
waypoints.content:
Here they rerun three baselines themselves under one configuration. Full fine-tuning, one token per step, length 256.

The ordering doesn't change. 89.1 against 86.9 for the next best on GSM8K, 45.1 against 41.8 on MATH-500.

Nice that they reported both versions of the benchmark: the big sweep and the tightly controlled one. And it's nice that the numbers line up.
waypoints.notes: ~45 sec.

waypoints.title: Maybe why no one tried this before
waypoints.content:
But if you train the model as an autoregressive model, have you just destroyed the parallel decoding that was the point of using a diffusion model in the first place?

X axis is tokens per step, so further right is more parallel and faster. Blue is the original model, orange is after JustGRPO.

Not only does it survive, the gap gets *wider*. On MBPP it's +10.6 points at one token per step and +25.5 at around five.

Their read is that AR training gives a more robust distribution, so it holds up better once you start approximating with parallel sampling. Speed advantage intact, accuracy advantage growing.

waypoints.title: And it isn't slower to train
waypoints.content:
Exact likelihood should cost more per step than an approximation, and it does. Diffusion models have to evaluate each position separately rather than in one causal pass.

Doesn't matter much. Accuracy against wall clock, JustGRPO matches the approximation-based baseline's peak and keeps going while that one saturates.

There's also a cheap variant. Since reasoning is steered by a sparse set of high-entropy tokens, only compute the probability ratio at the top 25% highest-entropy positions and skip 75% of the work. Trains faster, does no worse. Nice reuse of their own finding as an engineering trick.

For scale, all of this is 16 H100s for 125 steps.
waypoints.notes: ~1 min.

waypoints.title: Appendix B. Is it just a temperature artifact?
waypoints.content:
They compared the two modes at one temperature, 0.6. Temperature controls diversity, which is exactly what Pass\@k measures. Maybe arbitrary order just wants a different temperature?

Six panels sweeping temperature from 0.3 to 1.5.

The two modes really do behave differently. AR peaks around 0.6 and falls apart by 1.5. Arbitrary order peaks at higher temperatures, which fits their story, since if you're suppressing uncertainty you need more noise to compensate.

**Bottom right is the optimal temperature for each model.**
waypoints.notes: ~1.5 min. This was my main objection, so present it as such.

waypoints.title: Appendix B. Better samplers, and where they end up
waypoints.content:
This is the result I'd put money on being the most consequential one in the paper, and it's buried.

Confidence isn't the only rule for picking what to unmask. They try two better ones, top-*k* margin and negative entropy, on HumanEval.

Pass\@128 goes confidence 66.9, top-*k* margin 77.5, negative entropy 80.0, AR 83.0. So better samplers close most of the gap. None of them close it.

Then the right-hand panel, which is the part I keep chewing on. They correlate per-problem accuracy against AR order. Confidence 0.90, top-*k* margin 0.93, negative entropy **0.97**.

**The better a sampler gets, the more it behaves like left to right.** That's a rather different framing from the title. It isn't that flexibility is bad. It's that every good decoding rule anyone has found is converging on something AR gives you for free.
waypoints.notes: ~1.5 min. Appendix B.2, Figure 11. Don't skip this one, it sets up the order-space slide later.

waypoints.title: Appendix D. What about random order?
waypoints.content:
This one complicates the story and I think it's the most interesting appendix.

If flexibility is the problem, fully random order should be even worse. If confidence-based ordering is the problem, random might be better.

Pass@128 on GSM8K. Confidence 97.0, random 97.5, AR 99.0. Random is fine on coverage.

Pass@1 is where it dies. Confidence 78.6, random 43.3, AR 78.0. And under RL, random order reaches 82.2 against 89.1 for AR.

So the ranking isn't monotonic in flexibility. Left to right wins, confidence-based is next, random is worst. Which means left to right isn't winning because it's *rigid*. It's winning because it matches the direction the reasoning actually flows.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. Most interesting appendix. This is where the title gets complicated.

waypoints.title: What broken output looks like
waypoints.content:
This is why random order collapses on single-shot accuracy. An actual rollout from their run.

The model is asked to write token 30 when only token 1 exists. The LaTeX comes out with dangling operators and missing operands. It isn't a wrong answer, it's structurally broken text.

Broken output never earns a reward, so RL learns nothing from it.

The practical lesson is that a decoding order has to respect the dependency structure of whatever you're writing. Language mostly flows forward, so forward order is a good default.
waypoints.notes: ~1 min. Read the LaTeX out loud, it gets a laugh.

waypoints.title: Appendix E. Nothing else broke
waypoints.content:
Last worry. Did training in AR mode quietly turn it into a worse general model?

MMLU 65.5 to 65.8. MMLU-Pro 37.0 to 36.7. HellaSwag 74.6 to 74.8. ARC-C 88.5 to 87.5.

Flat, within noise in both directions. So this is really touching how the model *explores* during reasoning and not what it knows.

Consistent with the scaffold framing. The constraint shapes the search, not the representation.
waypoints.notes: ~45 sec. Ties back to 'scaffold'.

waypoints.title: What I'd push on
waypoints.content:
Things I'd want to argue about.

**The comparison isn't flexibility against rigidity.** It's one specific greedy heuristic against left to right. Confidence-based remasking is a choice, and Appendix B shows better samplers close some of the gap. The best one correlates 0.97 with AR behavior, which almost reads as "the better your sampler gets, the more it acts like left to right."

**Everything here is math and code**, where dependency really does run forward. On sudoku, which earlier work cites, arbitrary order *wins*. So the honest claim is narrower than the title.

**Pass@k at 128 samples is a strange construct.** It rewards a model for occasionally being right, and it's sensitive to temperature and to how you sample. Reasonable as a ceiling proxy, but it's a proxy.

**They never test their own scaffold at test time.** Table 1 is generated with confidence-based remasking in blocks of 32. So the AR-trained model is evaluated in arbitrary order, and nobody reports the obvious control, which is decoding it AR as well. That's a one-line experiment and its absence is strange.

And their own best line is buried in related work, highlighted here. Order carries structural information beyond content. That's a more interesting claim than "flexibility is a trap."
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. Start moving toward discussion.

waypoints.title: So is left to right special, or just well aligned?
waypoints.content:
The title says flexibility is a trap. But look at what actually got tested. Three orders and one knob.

| order | Pass@1 | Pass@128 | after RL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| left to right | 78.0 | **99.0** | **89.1** |
| confidence-first | **78.6** | 97.0 | — |
| fully random | 43.3 | 97.5 | 82.2 |

*GSM8K, LLaDA-Instruct, appendix D.*

Random is the informative row. If **rigidity** were the active ingredient, a fixed random permutation should do about as well as left to right, and it doesn't, it falls apart. If **freedom** were the ingredient, random should beat both. It doesn't either.

So the winning property is neither. It's *agreement with the dependency structure of whatever you're writing.* Left to right wins on math and code because math and code mostly flow forward. On sudoku and zebra puzzles, where constraints run in every direction, the earlier work they cite finds arbitrary order wins.

There's a theory-side hint too, one line in related work. Someone has argued that training on *uniform* permutations gives a strictly looser approximation to the data distribution than committing to a fixed order. If that's right, the problem was never freedom at inference. It was asking one network to be good at every order at once.

Which leaves a large space nobody has swept:

- **Hard-first.** Decode the *highest*-entropy slot each step, the exact inverse of what everyone does. Their own mechanism predicts this preserves the forks. It might also produce nonsense, and honestly I can't tell which.
- **Outline first.** Commit a skeleton, then fill it in. The paper notes dLLMs already do sketch-first spontaneously; nobody has made it a training scaffold.
- **Dependency order.** For code, def-before-use or AST order. For proofs, the dependency graph. Left to right is a crude approximation of both.
- **Decode then revise.** Their own closing appendix note points here and stops.

Left to right may simply be the best-aligned order we happen to have a name for.
waypoints.notes: ~2 min. This is the new one. Land the random-order row hard, it's what kills both simple stories. Then open question 1 in the discussion.

waypoints.title: Does any of this tell us about people?
waypoints.content:
Here's the case for **yes**.

The mechanism is described in ordinary cognitive language and it isn't a stretch. When you can choose what to work on, you do the easy parts first, and by the time you reach the hard decision the easy parts have already made it for you. Anyone who has written the methods section before the argument knows this feeling.

It has real analogues. Premature closure in clinical diagnosis. Path dependence and anchoring. Einstellung, where an early frame forecloses the search. The specific claim, that avoiding a hard decision doesn't remove the decision but silently makes it, is a testable hypothesis about people.

The measurement lesson transfers cleanly too. Single-shot performance and repeated-sampling ceiling gave opposite answers here.

And the **scaffold** result is the strongest bridge to this room. Constrain the process during learning, remove the constraint at performance, keep the gain. That's worked-example fading, and it's a rare case where we can see *why* the constraint helps, by shaping what gets explored.

Here's the case for **no**.

There isn't one human in this paper. The mechanism is a property of a decoding heuristic in an architecture nobody chose for psychological plausibility. Nobody claims masked diffusion is how people generate language. And if a different sampler gives a different answer, that's a bad sign for a claim about cognition.

The honest middle is that this is a hypothesis generator, not evidence. It shows the mechanism is possible in *some* generative system, which isn't nothing when the alternative is armchair speculation. But possible in a transformer is a long way from true in people.
waypoints.notes: ~3 min. The centerpiece. Don't rush. Then open the floor.

waypoints.title: Discussion
waypoints.content:
Five things I'd like to fight about.

**1.** Is left to right *uniquely* good, or just well aligned? They tested three orders. If the winning property is agreement with dependency structure rather than rigidity, some other constrained order should beat it. Hard-first, outline-first and dependency order are all untried. What would you bet on, and what would the equivalent be for a task that isn't math?

**2.** Is "the order you commit to things shapes what you can discover" a real cognitive claim, or does it only make sense for a system that generates text token by token?

**3.** If we wanted to test it in people, what's the design? Something that manipulates whether participants can choose the order they resolve subproblems, and measures the *diversity* of solutions rather than accuracy?

**4.** Pass@1 and Pass@128 disagreed here. Where does the same thing bite us? Single-shot writing assessment, one clinical interview, one item per construct?

**5.** The one I keep going back and forth on. Does a finding about a model count as evidence about cognition, as an existence proof about information processing in general, or as neither?
waypoints.notes: Leave this up for the ~30 min discussion.
